two cases:
∙ a highly eccentric orbit, for which a ≫  b, would have a value of e nearing 1, 
and the orbital shape would be a long and skinny ellipse;
∙ a low eccentricity orbit tends toward a circular shape for which a = b = p = r 
and e = 0.
The circular orbit is really just a special case of the elliptical orbit.
A Canadian spacecraft used for TV communications has been put into a highly elliptical 
orbit, called a Molniya orbit, with the following characteristics: the minimum orbital altitude 
(at perigee) is 400 km, the maximum orbital altitude (at apogee) is 41,800 km, and the 
eccentricity is 0.75. Determine the orbital parameters for this orbit, specifically a, b, and p. 
■ Solution
It is very important to recognize that “orbital altitude” refers to the height of the space -
craft above the surface of the gravitating body, but “orbital radius” refers to the distance 
from the center of the body; for an Earth orbiting spacecraft, they differ by the radius 
of the Earth. So first, we calculate the orbital radius at perigee and that at apogee, 
approximating the radius of the Earth as REarth = 6400 km:
 rmin = rperi = REarth + hperi = 6400 + 400 = 6800 km
similarly,
 rmax = rapo = REarth + hapo = 6400 + 41,800 = 48,200 km

8.5.2 Kepler’s Second Law
In equal times, the areas swept out by the radius vector of a satellite are the same.
To prove Kepler’s second law, recall from Eq. (8.28) that the angular momen -
tum of a satellite, mr2  θ ̇   , is constant. Consider Fig. 8.8, which shows the radius 
vector r sweeping through an infinitesimally small angle dθ. The area of the 
small triangle swept out is dA =   1 _ 2   r ds. But ds can be written as r dθ, and thus 
dA =   1 _ 2   r2dθ. The time rate of change of the area swept out by the radius vec -
tor is then:
    dA ___ dt    =      1 _ 2  r2dθ _____ dt    =    1 __ 2   r2  θ ̇    (8.51)
Since the angular momentum  mr 2  θ ̇    is constant and m is constant, clearly r2  θ ̇    
must be constant. Hence, Eq. (8.51) shows that:    dA ___ dt    = constant, which proves 
Kepler’s second law.
One clear conclusion that can be drawn from this law is that since the 
distance r is changing continually as the satellite follows this elliptical path,  
the velocity must also be changing continually. In fact, the velocity must be

8.6.1 Orbital Shapes
Kepler’s study of planetary motion allowed him to induce the elliptical shape of 
the paths that all planets in our solar system follow and the velocity variation 
along their trajectories. These characteristics were discussed in Sec. 8.5 by relying 
on the mathematical formula called the orbit equation (Eq. 8.44) that was derived 
previously using basic physics. The amazing thing is that this orbit equation, 
though it was inspired by and certainly describes an elliptical orbit perfectly, also 
defines all the other types of orbits that can occur in a central gravitational field. 
The orbit equation in its simplest form is repeated here:
 r =    p __________  1 +  e cos θ    (8.44)
where p is the parameter of the orbit and e is the eccentricity. This allows one 
to calculate the orbital radius  r  at any angular position θ. The mathematical 
beauty of this equation comes from the fact that there are actually four differ -
ent orbital shapes and all four can be obtained, simply by varying the value of 
the eccentricity e:
If e = 0, the path is a circle.
If e < 1, the path is an ellipse.
If e = 1, the path is a parabola.
If e > 1, the path is a hyperbola.
Geometric details for these four different shapes are shown in Fig. 8.9. In each 
case, M is the central gravitating body located at the focus of the orbit, and m 
is the orbiting body shown at a representative position displaced an angle θ away 
from the major axis. As the value of e changes from 0 through 1 to larger and 
larger values, the shape evolves from a circle, to an ellipse, to a longer thinner 
ellipse, to an open parabola, and finally to a hyperbola that gets wider and wider. 
This progression happens consistent with the growth of the semimajor axis a, 
The period of revolution of the Earth about the Sun is 1 year or 365.256 days. The 
semimajor axis of the Earth’s orbit is 1.49527 × 10 11 m. The semimajor axis of the 
orbit of Mars is 2.2783 × 10 11 m. Calculate the period of Mars.
■ Solution
From Kepler’s third law, we have
 τ2 = τ1   (  a2 __ a1
  )  
  3 __ 2  
   = 365.256    (  2.2783 _______ 1.49527  )  
  3 __ 2  
   = 686.96 days
So a year on Mars is roughly 687 earth days or about 1.88 earth years.

closed orbit, the orbiting body will eventually come back around, while for an 
open orbit, the orbiting body will never be seen again.

8.6.2 Orbital Energy
Basic physics would indicate that the type of path a spacecraft follows, and thus 
the value of e, is governed by the difference between the kinetic energy of the 
vehicle and its potential energy, with the expectation that if kinetic energy is 

===== PDF PAGE 708 =====
too high (vehicle going very fast), it is likely to escape the gravitational pull of 
the planet. To prove this, we will derive an expression for kinetic energy based 
on the velocity of the vehicle, and an expression for potential energy based on 
the position of the vehicle in the gravitational field. We will then calculate the 
difference between these two quantities, and obtain an expression for e.
Consider first the kinetic energy, T, of the spacecraft:

Now that we have an expression for kinetic energy in terms of e, we need to 
consider the potential energy of the orbiting body. It should be noted at this

convenient because if we define total energy, H, as the sum of kinetic and 
potential energy, the sign of H will be an indicator of which of these two 
quantities is larger in absolute value.
The potential energy, denoted as U, can be written in terms of e using

The sum of kinetic energy and potential energy, i.e., the total energy H, can 
thus be written
 H = T + U =    1 __ 2    m     μ __ p    (1 + 2 e cos θ + e2) − m     μ __ p    (1 + e cos θ) (8.64)
With a bit of manipulation, Eq. (8.64) becomes
 H = −    1 __ 2    m     μ __ p    (1 − e2) (8.65)
And solving Eq. (8.65) for e, we get 
 e =   √
__________
 1 +    2p ___ m μ   H     (8.66) 
This expression is the desired result, giving the eccentricity e in terms of the total 
energy H. If we now recognize that the constant   (  2p ___ m μ  )   is always positive, then 
the second term under the radical has the same sign as H. As a result, if the 
kinetic energy is less than the potential energy, then H < 0 and e < 1. If the 
kinetic and potential energies are equal, then H = 0 and e = 1. And if the kinetic 
energy is larger than the potential energy, then H > 0 and e > 1. This is consis -
tent with what we expected and consistent with the orbital shapes discussed 
above: for e < 1, the orbit is closed and the orbiting body remains trapped in the 
gravitational well of the central body; while for e ≥ 1, the orbit is open and the 
orbiting body is going fast enough that it can escape. These relationships are 
summarized in the following table:
Type of Trajectory Eccentricity e Energy Relation Result
Ellipse (closed) e < 1    1 __ 2    mV2 <    GMm _____ r   Not enough kinetic energy 
to escape ( H < 0)
Parabola (open) e = 1    1 __ 2    mV2 =    GMm _____ r   Exactly enough kinetic 
energy to escape ( H = 0)
Hyperbola (open) e > 1    1 __ 2    mV2 >    GMm _____ r   Plenty of kinetic energy  
to escape ( H > 0)
From this, we draw the important conclusion that a vehicle intended to escape 
from the gravitational well of the Earth and travel into deep space on a para -
bolic or hyperbolic trajectory must be launched so that its kinetic energy after 
burnout of the last stage of the launch vehicle is equal to or greater than its 
potential energy—a conclusion that makes intuitive sense even without the 
preceding derivation.
8.6.3 Orbital Velocities
A spacecraft designed for planetary exploration, heading toward the moons of 
Jupiter, for example, would most likely be launched on a multistage launch 
vehicle that would accelerate the spacecraft at least to escape velocity, Vesc, so 

===== PDF PAGE 710 =====
that it can depart the Earth and travel through interplanetary space. This neces -
sary velocity can actually be calculated quite easily simply by setting the 
kinetic energy of the vehicle equal to its potential energy, as discussed above:
    1 __ 2    mV2 =    GMm _____ r    (8.67)
Solving for V from this equation, we obtain Vesc:
 Vesc =   √
_____
 2   GM ____ r      =   √
___
 2   μ __ r      (8.68)
Note that this velocity is independent of the mass of the spacecraft itself, and 
in fact only depends on the gravitational constant of the planet from which it 
is escaping, and the initial distance, r, away from that planet. It makes sense 
that the further away from the planet you are initially, the lower the velocity 
you need to escape. Achieving exactly this velocity would put the spacecraft 
on a parabolic trajectory away from the Earth, while any velocity greater than 
this would result in a hyperbolic trajectory.
Consider now the case of a spacecraft designed to orbit the Earth at a 
constant altitude, perhaps for the purpose of obtaining precise meteorological 
data on cloud heights, for example. This would necessitate a circular orbit, and 
the required velocity can be determined simply by setting the eccentricity e 
equal to zero in Eq. (8.65) for H:
 H = −     1 __ 2    m     μ __ p    (1 − e2) = −     1 __ 2    m     μ __ p    (8.69)
Notice that for a circular orbit, the orbit equation, Eq. (8.44), just becomes  
r = p when a value of e = 0 is used. In other words, it is a statement that the 
orbital radius is constant and equal in value to the parameter p. But H is also, 
by definition, the difference between kinetic energy and potential energy:
 H =    1 __ 2    mV2 −    GMm _____ r    =    1 __ 2    mV2 −     μm ___ r    (8.70)
Equating these two expressions and recognizing again that GM = μ, we can 
solve for Vcirc:
 Vcirc =   √

This expression clearly shows that circular orbit velocity is less than escape 
velocity, which certainly makes sense, and the difference is exactly a factor of

increases its velocity by firing its engine, that velocity change will alter the 
orbit to an ellipse with the apogee further and further away until, as Vesc is 
achieved, the apogee distance goes to infinity.

8.6.4 The Vis-Viva Equation
Perhaps the most important characteristic of an object moving through space, 
at least in terms of trajectory determination, is its velocity, a quantity closely 
related to its total energy. In this section, we will derive the vis-viva equation 
which provides a simple means of calculating velocity anywhere along a trajec -
tory, knowing only the distance from the central body and the shape of the 
orbit. The name of this equation comes from the Latin words “vis” meaning 
“force” and “viva” meaning “live,” so named because the equation quantifies 
the motion of a body presumably being acted on by “live forces” moving it. 
These forces were considered fundamentally different from “vis mortua,” “dead 
forces” that when acting on a body would produce no active work but only 
pressure, such as “dead weight,” a term that is still in use today. We now know, 
of course, that the force that moves the planets through the sky is exactly the 
same as that which produces dead weight, and that force is gravity. Nevertheless, 
the name of the equation remains.
Remember first that the total energy of a body in a central gravitational 
field is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies as discussed above, and 
this total energy is H:
 H = T + U =    1 __ 2    mV2 −    GMm _____ r    (8.72)
 8.6 Orbital Energy and the Vis-Viva Equation 695

===== PDF PAGE 715 =====
696 CHAPTER 8 Space Flight (Astronautics)
Let us now define the specific energy , Et, which is the total energy per unit 
mass, H/m:
 Et =    H __ m    =    1 __ 2    V2 −    GM ____ r    =    1 __ 2     V2 −    μ __ r    (8.73)
For motion in a central force field, Et is constant and has the same sign as H 
used previously. Thus, the following statements are true:
∙ if Et < 0, the orbit is an ellipse (or a circle);
∙ if Et = 0, the orbit is a parabola;
∙ if Et > 0, the orbit is a hyperbola.
One of the more surprising aspects of spacecraft motion along a conic section is 
that the specific energy Et is fully defined by the semimajor axis of the orbital 
path. To prove this, recall Eq. (8.65) written in terms of specific energy, Et = H/m: 
 Et = −     1 __ 2       μ __ p    (1 − e2) (8.74)
And from Sec. 8.5, Eq. (8.48) stated:
 a =    p ______ 
1 −  e2   
Inverting this expression and substituting it in Eq. (8.74) yields:
 Et = −     1 __ 2        μ __ a     (8.75)
This result shows that the semimajor axis a is an exclusive measure of the 
specific energy of the orbiting body.
Equating these two expressions for Et, Eq. (8.73) and Eq. (8.75), we have
    1 __ 2   V2 −    μ __ r    = −     1 __ 2        μ __ a    
or
 V2 = μ   (  2 __ r   −    1 __ a  )  
or
 V =   √
__________
 μ  (  2 __ r   −    1 __ a  )      (8.76)
This is the vis-viva equation or the energy equation. When an orbiting body is 
at a location specified by r on a given orbital trajectory, the magnitude of the 
velocity can be calculated directly at that location—and this tremendously use -
ful result applies to all four types of orbits. 
In order to apply this formula, the semimajor axis a must be known. In all 
cases, a is the distance from the center of the conic section to the periapsis 

===== PDF PAGE 716 =====
point. For a circular orbit, a is simply the radius. For an elliptical orbit, a can 
be calculated a number of ways, knowing the eccentricity and parameter of the 
orbit, or knowing the periapsis and apoapsis radii, for example. The semimajor 
axis for a parabola is infinite, which may seem like a problem but actually 
results in a finite and correct expression in Eq. (8.76) above. Finally, for the 
hyperbolic orbit, there are actually two mirror-image hyperbolas, and the center 
lies between them, as shown in Fig. 8.9, such that the distance from the center 
to the periapsis is negative.

8.7 ORBITAL MANEUVERING
Travel in space generally requires piecing together a series of orbital trajec -
tories, each segment of which is a section of one of the orbits that we have 
discussed in the previous parts of this chapter. Orbital maneuvering is the 
process of transferring from one trajectory segment to the next; in all cases a 
change in velocity is needed to accomplish this transfer. It is critical for mis -
sion planning to be able to calculate well ahead of time exactly how much 
change in velocity is needed for each maneuver, because every change in 
velocity requires expending some amount of fuel, and all necessary fuel must 
be loaded and launched with the spacecraft, at least at this current time. When 
there are fuel depots in orbit where a spacecraft can refuel, this may become 
less critical but for the moment, there are no gas stations in space. 
The “cost” of every maneuver is therefore measured in terms of how much 
change in velocity, often referred to as “delta- V” (or Δ V), is needed. This sec -
tion will discuss the process and necessary Δ V to accomplish two types of 
maneuvers: a transfer between two coplanar orbits, and a change of inclination 
of an orbit (a plane change). While these are both very useful orbital maneu -
vers, we are only touching the surface of the complexity and variety of types 
of maneuvers that can be performed in space.
Suppose the spacecraft discussed in the last couple examples is actually an interplan -
etary probe that after orbiting the Earth a few times to deploy antennas and solar arrays 
and check out all systems, now must be inserted into a hyperbolic escape orbit to head 
toward the outer solar system. An upper stage motor will be fired to achieve this new 
orbit when the spacecraft is at a true anomaly of 120°, and the hyperbolic orbit is 
defined by a value of a = −11,500 km. How much change in velocity is necessary for 
the spacecraft to achieve its new orbit ?
■ Solution
From Example 8.10 above, we know that the spacecraft will be starting the insertion 
burn traveling at an initial velocity of 5.34 km/s at θ = 120°.
The final velocity that the spacecraft needs to achieve at the end of the burn can 
be calculated using the vis-viva equation with the same orbital radius r but changing 
the value of a to be that for the desired hyperbolic orbit:
 V =  √
_________
 μ (  2 __ r   −    1 __ a  )    =   √
______________________________________
     3.986 × 10 14 (  2 __________ 
13.7 × 10 6   −    1 ____________  
(−11.5 × 10 6)
  )     = 9.63 km/s
The necessary change in velocity that the upper stage has to produce is therefore
 Δ V = Vfinal − Vinitial = 9.63 − 5.34 = 4.39 km/s
Note that to do this calculation, we have assumed that the entire burn is done at  
r = 13.7  ×  10 6 m ; in other words, the change in velocity is instantaneous. This is 
generally a good assumption.

8.7.1  Coplanar Orbital Maneuvers and the Hohmann Transfer
Consider a spacecraft in a given initial elliptical orbit, labeled orbit 1 in Fig. 8.13, 
with a major axis as shown. The goal is to put this spacecraft on a new orbital 
path, labeled orbit 2 and defined by major axis 2. The two orbits intersect at 
Point A, so it is at this point that the orbit change maneuver will occur when  
the spacecraft fires its maneuvering engine and produces the necessary Δ V. 
Conceptually the process is quite simple: if the spacecraft comes into Point A 
with an initial velocity vector V1, tangent to orbit 1, it must change to a new 
velocity V2, tangent to orbit 2 at this same point. We are making the assumption 
that the velocity change can occur instantaneously by applying a single impulsive 
Δ V at that point. Writing this in terms of vectors:
 Δ V = V2 −  V1 (8.77)
If we now assume that the angle between the two velocity vectors (i.e., between 
the tangents to the two orbits at Point A) is α, we can write the following 
scalar equation using the law of cosines:
 (Δ V)2 =   V  1  2   +   V  2  2   − 2 V1V2 cos α (8.78)
To fully determine this maneuver, one would need to know all the characteristics 
of the initial orbit and all the characteristics of the final orbit (especially, for 
example, their semimajor axes, a1 and a2), as well as the exact location of the 
point of intersection A. If we knew all this, it would be quite straightforward to 
calculate the magnitudes of the two velocity vectors, using the vis-viva equation:

assume for this discussion that α = 0°, which physically means that the two 
orbits are tangent to each other at the point of intersection. While this will 
not generally be the case in real-world applications, it is a situation that arises 
often enough to be quite useful and it certainly simplifies the calculation.

be performed where the two orbits are tangent. This is not an unusual occurrence, 
for example, if one were to transfer from a circular orbit to an elliptical orbit at 
either the periapsis or apoapsis of the elliptical orbit. Example 8.12 illustrates a

So while the eccentricity of the orbit is quite small, the satellite may be higher than its 
desired location by as much as 530 km, which is quite significant for a spacecraft 
nominally in a 250 km altitude orbit. The operational requirements for this scientific 
satellite would determine whether this much eccentricity and variation in orbital altitude 
is a problem for the mission or not, but clearly the takeaway is that Δ V requirements 
must be precisely determined and executed because even seemingly small inaccuracies 
can lead to large offsets in location.

The above discussion addressed the transfer between two intersecting orbits 
(and, in fact, further specialized that the two orbits shall be tangent at their point 
of intersection). Let us now consider the necessary maneuvers that would need 
to be executed to transfer from an orbit to another non-intersecting orbit, as 
illustrated in Fig. 8.15. In this figure, we are again considering a transfer from 
one elliptical orbit to another elliptical orbit, but not only is there no point of 
tangency, there is actually no point of intersection at all. So the procedure would 
require identifying a transfer trajectory shown notionally as the dotted path from 
point 1 to point 2. To follow this path would require first an impulsive change 
in velocity, Δ V1 at point 1, to get on the transfer trajectory, and then a second 
impulsive Δ V2 at point 2, to get on orbit 2 instead of continuing along the trans-
fer path. Note that Δ V, which is the magnitude of the vector Δ V, is always a 
positive number regardless of the direction of that vector. So the total Δ V is 
simply the sum of these two magnitudes, Δ V1 + Δ V2. To calculate the total fuel 
requirements for a mission, it is this sum of all necessary Δ V’s that is used. The 
sign or direction of an impulsive thrust maneuver is determined by the orienta -
tion of the spacecraft during the burn, which can be precisely controlled. Thus 
to speed up, for example, the engine would be pointed back along the flight path 
when firing, while to slow down, the vehicle would be rotated 180° so the engine 
can fire into the flight path direction.
Determining the two Δ V’s for this generic transfer is beyond the scope of 
this textbook, and also does not necessarily represent a minimum required Δ V. 
So, again both for simplicity and because we are trying to calculate a minimum 
Δ V, let’s consider the special case of transferring from one circular orbit to 
another coplanar circular orbit about the same central body. This minimum-
energy maneuver is called a Hohmann transfer  and has the following 
characteristics if the transfer is from a lower circular orbit (radius r1) to a higher 
circular orbit (radius r2)—see Fig. 8.16:
∙ depart the first circular orbit tangentially at r1 (point 1);
∙ as soon as Δ V1 is applied, this departure point becomes the periapsis of the 
elliptical transfer orbit;

 8.7 Orbital Maneuvering 705
8.7.2 Plane Change Maneuver
Spacecraft are most easily launched due east into an orbital plane that is at the 
same inclination as the latitude of the launch site: eastward, because this takes 
maximum advantage of the eastward rotational velocity of the Earth; and incli -
nation equal to the latitude of the launch site because the orbital plane has to 
include both the center of the earth and the launch site itself. Any launch 
azimuth other than due east results in an orbit with a higher inclination than 
the launch site latitude. The higher the inclination, the smaller the benefit of 
the Earth’s rotation, so launching to a higher inclination requires more energy 
and results in smaller payloads. But, without a specific plane change maneuver, 
nothing can be launched into an orbital inclination lower than the latitude of 
the launch site. 
For example, when the United States first started collaborating with Russia 
on building the International Space Station (ISS), one of the early discussions 
was the question of what the orbital inclination of the ISS should be. Payloads 
launched from Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral, Florida, are maxi -
mized if they go into an orbit at a 28.5° inclination, matching the latitude of 
Cape Canaveral. From Baikonur, Kazakhstan, the Russian launch site, payloads 
must be launched into a high inclination orbit at 51.6° or higher; nothing 
launched from there could be inserted into a lower inclination orbit directly. 

===== PDF PAGE 725 =====
706 CHAPTER 8 Space Flight (Astronautics)
Thus, the decision was made to put ISS at an orbital inclination of 51.6°, so 
that both nations could launch components, supplies and crew, although the 
U.S. payload sizes would be reduced due to the higher inclination launches.
To determine the Δ V necessary for a plane change maneuver, first consider 
the case of a spacecraft in a circular orbit that needs to transfer to an identical 
circular orbit but at a different inclination, where the change in inclination is 
an angle Δ i. Independent of where along the orbit the impulse Δ V is applied, 
the geometry of this situation is as shown in Fig. 8.17. Notice that the magnitude 
of the velocity is the same at Point A whether you are on orbit 1 or orbit 2, 
because the two orbits have the same orbital radius and thus the same velocity. 
The direction of the two velocity vectors is different, of course, and the differ -
ence is the vector Δ V. Notice that if you split the angle Δ i into two half angles 
Δ i/2, as shown by the dotted line, and consider one of the two triangles thus 
formed, you can easily write the following expression:
    Δ V ___ 2    = V sin   (  Δ i ___ 2  )    or  Δ V = 2 V sin   (  Δ i ___ 2  )   (8.87)
This expression, which was obtained for circular orbits, has to be slightly 
modified in order to calculate the Δ V necessary to transfer from an elliptical 
orbit to an identical elliptical orbit at a different inclination:
 where Vθ = component of  
V perpendicular to r vector (8.88)
The qualitative reason for this modification is that the angular momentum, h, 
of the orbit only depends on the component of orbital velocity in the θ direc-
tion ( h = rV θ), and when the orbital inclination is changed, it is actually the 
momentum vector h that must be rotated.
One clear result of this boxed expression is that in order to minimize the 
Δ V necessary to perform a plane change maneuver, the impulse should be 
applied at the point along the orbit where Vθ is minimum. For a circular orbit, 
Vθ = V throughout the orbit so it does not matter where a plane change

8.8 INTERPLANETARY TRAJECTORIES
The only way that a spacecraft launched from the earth can fly in interplanetary 
space is for it to achieve escape velocity, given by Eq. (8.68) and repeated here:

where the burnout velocity is larger than that given by Eq. ( 8.68), the trajectory 
will be a hyperbola. Almost all interplanetary space vehicles are initially 
launched in hyperbolic trajectories. In this section we are interested in the flight 
path taken by a space vehicle launched from the earth with a mission to visit 
one or more planets in the solar system. Because the initial trajectory after 
launch is hyperbolic, we need to pause and examine some of the features of a 
hyperbolic trajectory.

8.8.2 Sphere of Influence
The hyperbolic flight path discussed in Sec. 8.8.1 assumes that the space vehi -
cle is moving under the gravitational attraction of a single planet. This is called 
the two-body problem, with motion of the spacecraft of mass m in the vicinity 
of the planet of mass M where the only force acting on the spacecraft is the 
gravitational force between m and M. The additional gravitational forces 

===== PDF PAGE 730 =====
between the spacecraft and the sun, the moon, or other planets are neglected. 
This is a reasonable assumption as long as the spacecraft is within the sphere 
of influence of the planet of mass M. For space flight within our solar system, 
the gravitational attraction of the sun can play a major role. A conventional 
definition of the sphere of influence for a planet is the region where the grav -
itational force of the planet is greater than that of the sun. For example, the 
radius of the sphere of influence of the Earth is 9.25 × 10 5 km; this is much 
larger than the radius of the Earth, which is 6.4 × 10 3 km, but much smaller 
than the distances between the orbits of the planets, such as the distance of 
4.19 × 10 7 km between the orbits of the Earth and Venus and 7.77 × 10 7 km 
between the orbits of the Earth and Mars. For an extensive discussion of the 
sphere of influence and a tabulation of sphere of influence radii for all the 
planets in our solar system, see the book by Griffin and French (listed in this 
chapter’s bibliography).
8.8.3 Heliocentric Trajectories
Once a space vehicle launched from a planet (labeled the departure planet ) 
leaves the sphere of influence of that planet, the vehicle moves primarily under 
the gravitational attraction of the sun. If the mission of the space vehicle is to 
travel to another planet (labeled the target planet ), it enters a transfer orbit 
between the respective orbits of the two planets around the sun. This flight path 
is sketched in Fig. 8.19. The motion of the planets and the space vehicle illus -
trated in Fig. 8.19 is relative to the sun—in contrast to our previous discussions 
of motion along elliptical and hyperbolic flight paths taken relative to a planet 
(such as an orbit around the Earth). The transfer orbit shown in Fig. 8.19 is an 
orbit about the sun . The space vehicle enters this transfer orbit at point 1 with 
a velocity V1 relative to the sun that is the vector sum of the velocity of the

excess velocity on arrival at the target planet, V∞, tp:
 V2 = Vtp + V∞, tp (8.93)
In the preliminary design of an interplanetary space mission, the transfer 
orbit shown in Fig. 8.19 is frequently taken as a minimum-energy Hohmann 
transfer (see Sec. 8.7.1), although it does not have to be so restricted. The 
heliocentric transfer trajectory can be tailored to whatever the mission designer 
wants. It does not even have to be coplanar with the orbits of the departure or 
arrival planets. See the books by Griffin and French and by Brown (listed in 
this chapter’s bibliography) for in-depth discussion of such matters.
8.8.4 Method of Patched Conics
The detailed design of an interplanetary mission involves a numerical solution 
for the space vehicle flight path, solving the equations of motion and taking into 
account the multibody problem of the simultaneous influence of the gravitational 
fields of the sun, planets, and various moons. Such matters are well beyond the 
scope of this book. For the preliminary design of an interplanetary mission, 
however, a much simpler approach, called the method of patched conics, is used 
frequently. This method is carried out in three steps:
1. The heliocentric transfer orbit is computed first. The spheres of influence 
of both the departure and arrival planets are so small compared to the 
distance between the planets that the computation of the heliocentric 
transfer orbit simply ignores these planets.
2. The hyperbolic trajectory at the departure planet then defines the value 
of V∞  required at the departure end of the transfer trajectory (at point 1 
in Fig. 8.19). See Eq. ( 8.92).
3. The spacecraft moving along its transfer orbit arrives at the target planet 
at point 2 in Fig. 8.19 with a hyperbolic excess velocity V∞, tp relative to 
the target planet [see Eq. ( 8.93)]. The resulting hyperbolic trajectory 
about the target planet is then calculated for this V∞, tp.
We have discussed the essential aspects of the trajectories identified in Steps 1–3 
in previous sections, so no further elaboration will be given here.
The method of patched conics is only an approximate preliminary design 
method. It assumes an abrupt change from one conic flight path to another at 
the sphere of influence radius, thus ignoring the gradual transition from one 
flight path to another. It gives reasonable predictions of Δ V for the mission but 

===== PDF PAGE 732 =====
frequently leads to errors of hours or even days in the flight time. It can be 
made by hand calculations, however, which is a tremendous advantage for quick 
feasibility assessments. For our purposes in this chapter, it illustrates the essen -
tial elements of the flight path of a spacecraft on an interplanetary mission.
8.8.5 Gravity-Assist Trajectories
Consider the case where a space vehicle in a heliocentric orbit, such as the 
dashed curve in Fig. 8.19, flies into the sphere of influence of an intermediate 
planet different from the final target planet. The resulting hyperbolic encounter 
relative to the intermediate planet is sketched in Fig. 8.20. The approach 
asymptote has a true anomaly of − θa, and the departure asymptote has a true 
anomaly of θa, as shown in Fig. 8.20. The trajectory of the space vehicle 
is turned through the angle ψ relative to the planet as a result of the encounter. 
The magnitudes of the approach and departure velocities are the same value, V∞ ; 
but the direction of the velocity vector is changed.
Now focus on this event as seen in the heliocentric frame of reference 
(such as in Fig. 8.19). Because the intermediate planet has a velocity in its 
orbit around the sun, the departure velocity of the space vehicle in the helio -
centric system is the vector sum of the departure velocity from the planet and 
the velocity of the planet itself. Therefore, the magnitude of the velocity of the

space vehicle in the heliocentric system after encounter with the planet will be 
different than before—that is, the energy of the space vehicle changes  as a 
result of this encounter. When the space vehicle gains energy, it does so at the 
expense of the energy of the planet, which is of little consequence because 
the mass of the planet M is much larger than that of the space vehicle m. The 
reverse occurs when the space vehicle loses energy to the planet.
The maneuver discussed here is called a gravity-assist maneuver , and the 
resulting trajectory is a gravity-assist trajectory. You might say that the planet 
acts as a slingshot to change the energy of the space vehicle. Gravity assist 
is vital to a deep-space mission where the initial impulse Δ V required to 
launch the space vehicle directly from the earth to its intended target planet 
is prohibitively large. An example is the Galileo mission to Jupiter, which 
involved a gravity-assist flyby of Venus, then two gravity-assist flybys of the 
earth before the spacecraft had enough energy to get to Jupiter. The two 
Voyager spacecraft also used the gravity-assist maneuver many times during 
their outbound exploration of the solar system. Their mission is described in 
detail in Sec. 8.8.6.
The effect of the gravity-assist maneuver on the velocity of the space 
vehicle is illustrated vectorially in Fig. 8.21. In Fig. 8.21a the arrival and 
departure velocities of the space vehicle relative to the planet are shown. The 
departure velocity V∞ D is the vector sum of the arrival velocity V∞ A and the 
change in velocity Δ V due to the turning angle ψ:
 V∞ D = V∞ A + Δ V (8.94)
The heliocentric velocities are shown in Fig. 8.21b. The velocity of the planet 
in the heliocentric system is Vp. The approach velocity of the space vehicle 
relative to the planet is V∞ A. Hence, the approach velocity of the space vehicle 
in the heliocentric systems is VSA:
 VSA = Vp + V∞ A (8.95)
After the encounter with the planet, the departure velocity of the space vehicle 
in the heliocentric system is VSD:
 VSD = Vp + V∞ D (8.96)

Alternatively,
 VSD = VSA + Δ V (8.97)
Clearly, the magnitude of the velocity of the space vehicle after encounter in 
the heliocentric system is different from that before encounter; the gravity-assist 
maneuver has changed the energy of the space vehicle. For the case shown in 
Fig. 8.20, the gravity-assist maneuver has increased the energy of the space 
vehicle. On a qualitative basis this makes sense. In Fig. 8.21b the planet is 
moving from left to right with velocity Vp. In Fig. 8.20, which is drawn relative 
to the planet, we note that the spacecraft is arriving with the arrival velocity 
V∞ A to the left side of the planet, which is the back or retreating side of the 
planet. As a result, when the spacecraft’s velocity is bent around to the departure 
velocity V∞ D, the impulse Δ V is in the same general direction as the velocity 
of the planet, and hence the spacecraft’s velocity (energy) in the heliocentric 
system is increased. You might say that the planet is dragging the spacecraft 
along with it for a while. The opposite would happen if the spacecraft arrived 
in front of the planet (to the right of M in Fig. 8.20); in this case the hyperbolic 
trajectory would curve in the opposite direction as that shown in Fig. 8.20, and 
the planet’s motion would slow down the spacecraft’s velocity, causing a loss 
of spacecraft energy. This is what is used for inner planetary missions such as 
to Mercury with a gravity-assist maneuver performed at Venus.
8.8.6  An Application: The Voyager Spacecraft—Their Design, 
Flight Trajectories, and Historical Significance
The Voyager 2 spacecraft is shown in Fig. 2.25 as an example of a classic 
spacecraft arrangement. The two almost identical spacecraft, Voyager 1 and 
Voyager 2, were designed, built, and operated by NASA’s Jet Propulsion 
Laboratory (JPL) in Pasadena, California. The Jet Propulsion Laboratory is 
owned and managed by the California Institute of Technology on behalf of 
NASA. The Voyager missions are part of NASA’s Heliophysics System 
Observatory, sponsored by the Heliophysics Division of the Science Mission 
Directorate at NASA Headquarters in Washington, D.C. Although similar, the 
two Voyagers were sent on different flight paths through the solar system and 
into deep space. This section details those different trajectories and discusses 
some of the design aspects and historical significance of the Voyagers.
The design of the Voyager spacecraft  was driven by one primary 
 requirement—the acquisition of new scientific data. In essence, the spacecraft 
were a type of space truck whose single purpose was to carry a load of spe -
cialized instruments, shown and identified in Fig. 2.25, along with the small 
vernier rockets needed for mid-course corrections in the flight trajectory. 
Because the flight trajectories would take the Voyagers to various planets 
and their moons, it was necessary to mount the instruments on an articulated 
instrument platform shown on the right side of the spacecraft in Fig. 2.25. 
On this articulated platform, the instruments had an unobstructed view of 
 8.8 Interplanetary Trajectories 715

===== PDF PAGE 735 =====
716 CHAPTER 8 Space Flight (Astronautics)
each planet with the planet at any position with respect to the spacecraft. The 
high gain antenna through which information and data is sent to and from 
the spacecraft, as seen at the top of the spacecraft in Fig. 2.25, is constantly 
pointing to the Earth.
The original mission of both Voyagers was to conduct close-up studies of 
Jupiter and Saturn, Saturn’s rings, and the larger moons of the two planets. For 
this two-planet mission the Voyagers were built to last five years. However, 
the mission to Jupiter and Saturn was so successful that Voyager 2 was re-
programmed remotely to last 12 years in order to fly past Uranus and Neptune 
as well. This extension was made possible by using gravity-assist maneuvers 
which allowed each spacecraft to swing from one planet to the other, picking 
up energy and velocity from each planet, and allowing the spacecraft to move 
to the next planet without using the onboard propulsion system.
Both spacecraft are on hyperbolic trajectories away from the sun, which 
have now carried them into the beginning of interstellar space. For this reason 
NASA renamed the project as the Voyager Interstellar Mission. Various instru -
ments that earlier had been turned off were turned back on, and by judicious 
use of power, the lifetime of the two spacecraft has been extended. The radio -
isotope thermoelectric generators powering the instruments on both Voyagers 1 
and 2 have been running down since their launch in 1977. By 2020, the instru -
ments on Voyager 1 must share power by rotating on and off. By 2025, its last 
instrument will be shut down for good.
To track the flight paths of both Voyagers 1 and 2 we start with their launch 
from the NASA Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral, Florida—Voyager 2 
on August 20, 1977, and Voyager 1 just 15 days later , on September 5, 1977. 
The Voyager missions were named based on which would arrive at Jupiter first, 
rather than which was launched first.  Both were launched on Titan-Centaur 
booster rockets. The flight trajectories of both Voyagers are sketched (not to 
scale) in Fig. 8.22. Examining the trajectory of Voyager 1, we have:

Termination shock
The last entry in the tabulation above is the month when the two Voyagers 
crossed the termination shock, a term that requires some explanation. The sun 
is surrounded by a large region called the heliosphere, which contains the solar 
wind, made up of plasma blown out from the sun. The heliosphere is a kind 
of “bubble” that contains the solar wind against the somewhat constant outside 
pressure of the interstellar medium, the hydrogen and helium gas and other 
matter that makes up our galaxy. Close to the sun, the solar wind is supersonic, 
at velocities from 300 to 800 km/s relative to the sun. (The speed of sound in 
the interstellar medium is approximately 100 km/s.) As the solar wind propa -
gates away from the sun, its velocity steadily decreases, and its pressure 
decreases with the square of the distance from the sun. Far enough away from 
the sun, the pressure from the interstellar medium is sufficient to slow the solar 
wind to the speed of sound, where a shock wave occurs. This shock is called 
the termination shock, across which there is compression, heating, and a change 
in the magnetic field. Voyager 1 encountered the termination shock in Decem -
ber 2004 at a distance of 94 astronomical units (AU) from the sun. (An 
astronomical unit is the average distance from the earth to the sun, equal to 
roughly 150 million km.) Almost three years later, in August 2007, Voyager 2 
passed through the termination shock. The other side of the termination shock, 
where the solar wind is subsonic and strongly interacts with the interstellar 
medium, is called the heliosheath. In turn, the outer surface of the heliosheath is 
the heliopause, beyond which there is just the interstellar  medium. On August 25, 
2012, an instrument on Voyager 1 recorded a sharp drop in cosmic rays that 
are  produced inside the heliosphere. After much scientific debate, that date is 
now  accepted as the exit of Voyager 1 from the heliosphere and its entry into 
interstellar space. (See Kerr, “It’s Official—Voyager Has Left The Solar System,” 
Sept. 13, 2013, pp. 1158–1159.) At that time, running out of power with its instru-
ments failing, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to enter interstellar 
space. Voyager 2 was not far behind and itself entered interstellar space on 
Nov. 5, 2018.
This section describing the flight of the Voyagers is intended to show the 
application of our discussions in earlier sections of Ch. 8 on the motion of 
spacecraft in space, where such motion is driven by the force of gravity only, 

===== PDF PAGE 738 =====
 8.9 Introduction to Atmospheric Entry 719
whether it be the gravitational field from the sun, from the earth, or from other 
planets in our solar system. The physics and mathematics of flight through 
space is one of the most important aspects of the study of aerospace engineer -
ing, and the flight of the Voyager spacecraft is a stellar example of how careful 
and clever trajectory planning can enhance the scientific data return from inter -
planetary spacecraft with very little additional fuel. This historical account of 
the Voyager “Grand Tour ” of our solar system represents just the beginning 
of space exploration and discovery.
8.9  INTRODUCTION TO ATMOSPHERIC  ENTRY 1
In all cases of contemporary crewed space vehicles, and with many uncrewed 
vehicles, it is necessary to terminate the orbit or trajectory at some time and  
return to the earth. Obviously this necessitates negotiating the atmosphere at 
high velocities. An orbital vehicle will enter the outer regions of the atmo -
sphere at a velocity close to 26,000 ft/s; a vehicle returning from a moon 
mission (such as an Apollo vehicle) will enter at an even higher velocity— 
nearly 36,000 ft/s. These velocities correspond to flight Mach numbers of 30 
or more! Such hypersonic flight conditions are associated with several uniquely 
difficult aerodynamic problems—so unique and difficult that they dominated 
the research efforts of aerodynamicists during the late 1950s and throughout 
the 1960s. The successful manned entries of the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo 
 vehicles were striking testimonials to the success of this hypersonic research. 
Some aspects of hypersonic vehicles are discussed in Ch. 10.
Consider a space vehicle in orbit about the earth, as shown in Fig. 8.23. 
We wish to terminate this orbit and land the vehicle somewhere on the earth’s 
surface. First the path of the vehicle is changed by firing a retrorocket, decreas -
ing the vehicle’s velocity. In terms of the orbit equation, Eq. (8.43) or (8.44), 
the retrorocket’s firing effectively changes the values of h and e so that the 
vehicle curves toward the earth. When the vehicle encounters the outer region 
of the atmosphere (portrayed by the dashed circle in Fig. 8.23), three types of 
entry paths are possible:
1. Ballistic entry. Here the vehicle has little or no aerodynamic lift. It falls 
through the atmosphere under the influence of drag and gravity, striking 
the surface at point a. The impact point is predetermined by the 
conditions at first entry to the atmosphere. The pilot has no control over 
his or her landing position during this ballistic trajectory. It literally is the 
same as falling to the surface. Before the Space Shuttle, virtually all 
entries of existing space vehicles were ballistic. (A slight exception might 
be the Apollo capsule, which at an angle of attack could generate a small 
1In much of the literature you will find references to earth reentry rather than earth entry. The word 
reentry implies that the space vehicle had entered the atmosphere before and now is doing so again. This 
is usually not true except for the Space Shuttle. So we will use the word entry here; it seems grammatically 
more correct, and it is in keeping with modern use.

===== PDF PAGE 739 =====
720 CHAPTER 8 Space Flight (Astronautics)
lift-to-drag ratio, L/D  < 1. However, for all practical purposes, this is still 
a ballistic entry vehicle.)
2. Glide entry.  Here the vehicle is essentially an airplane, generating a 
lift-to-drag ratio of 4 or larger. The vehicle enters the atmosphere at  
a high angle of attack (30° or more) and flies to the surface, landing 
at point b in Fig. 8.23. An example of such a lifting entry vehicle is 
Space Shuttle Orbiter, as shown in Fig. 2.22,  for which  the pilot can, 
in principle, choose the landing site and the vehicle can be landed 
intact, to be used again.
3. Skip entry. Here the vehicle generates a value of L/D between 1 and 4 
and uses this lifting ability to first graze the atmosphere, then slow down 
a bit, then pitch up so that the lift carries it back out of the atmosphere. 
This is repeated several times, much like a flat stone skipping over the 
surface of a pond, until finally the vehicle is slowed down appropriately 
and penetrates the atmosphere, landing at point c in Fig. 8.23. 
Unfortunately the  aerodynamic heating of a skip entry vehicle is 
inordinately large, and  therefore such an entry mode has never been 
used and is not contemplated in the future.
All these entry modes present two overriding technical concerns: maxi -
mum deceleration and aerodynamic heating. For the safety and comfort of the 
occupants of a crewed entry vehicle, the maximum deceleration should not 
exceed 5 times the acceleration of gravity—that is, 5 g’s. Furthermore, the 
aerodynamic heating of the vehicle should be low enough to maintain tolerable 
temperatures inside the capsule; if the vehicle is uncrewed, it still must be kept 
from burning up in the atmosphere.
Figure 8.23 Three types of entry paths: ( a) ballistic; ( b) glide; ( c) skip.


===== PDF PAGE 740 =====
Additionally,  there is another consideration in regard to the entry of 
crewed  space vehicles returning from lunar or planetary missions. Such 
vehicles will approach the earth with parabolic or hyperbolic trajectories, as 
shown in Fig. 8.24. If the vehicle is traveling along path A in Fig. 8.24, 
penetration of the atmosphere will be too rapid, and the maximum decelera -
tion will be too large. In contrast, if the vehicle is traveling along path B, 
it will not penetrate the atmosphere enough; the drag will be too low, the 
velocity will not decrease enough for the vehicle to be captured by the earth, 
and it will go shooting past, back into outer space, never to return again. 
Consequently, there is a narrow entry corridor  into which the vehicle must 
be guided for a successful return to the earth’s surface. This entry corridor 
is shown in Fig. 8.24, bounded above by the overshoot boundary  and below 
by the undershoot boundary.
8.9.1 Exponential Atmosphere
Because entry involves motion through the atmosphere, it is reasonable to 
expect entry performance to depend on the physical properties of the atmo -
sphere. Such properties have been discussed in Ch. 3, where the atmospheric 
temperature distribution is given in Fig. 3.4. Detailed entry trajectory calcula -
tions made on computers take into account the precise variation of the standard 
atmosphere as given in Ch. 3. However, for a first approximation, a completely 
isothermal atmosphere with a constant temperature equal to some mean of the

variation shown in Fig. 3.4 can be assumed. In this case the density variation 
with altitude is a simple exponential, as given by Eq. (3.10). [At this point the 
reader should review the derivation of Eq. (3.10).] Writing Eq. (3.10) with point 
1 at sea level, we obtain
    ρ _  ρ  0     =  e   −  g  0  h/(RT)   (8.98)
Equation (8.98) establishes the exponential model atmosphere. It agrees rea-
sonably well with the actual density variation of the earth’s standard atmosphere 
up to about 450,000 ft (about 140 km); above this height, the air is so thin that 
it has no meaningful influence on the entry trajectory. The exponential model 
atmosphere was used by NASA and other laboratories in the early studies of earth 
entry during the 1950s and early 1960s. We will adopt it here for the remainder 
of this chapter.

path, as usual. Summing forces parallel and perpendicular to the flight path

will not be given here; our intent has been simply to map out an approach to

more details from the NACA and NASA reports given in the bibliography at 
the end of this chapter.
After the preceding analysis is completed, what does the actual entry path 
look like? An answer is given in Fig. 8.27, which illustrates the variation of 
velocity (the abscissa) with density (the ordinate). Because ρ is a function of 

===== PDF PAGE 744 =====
altitude, h is also given on the ordinate. Thus Fig. 8.27 shows the entry path in 
terms of velocity versus altitude—a so-called velocity–altitude map for entry. 
Such velocity–altitude maps are frequently used in entry vehicle design and 
analysis. Examine Fig. 8.27 more closely. Imagine an entry vehicle just begin -
ning to penetrate the atmosphere. It is at a very high altitude and velocity, such 
as point a in Fig. 8.27. During the early portion of entry, the atmospheric density 
is so low that the drag is virtually insignificant; the vehicle penetrates the upper 
region of the atmosphere with only a small decrease in velocity, as shown from 
point a to point b. However, below the altitude denoted by point b, the air 
density rapidly increases, with an attendant marked increase in drag, causing 
the velocity to decrease rapidly. This is the situation at point c in Fig. 8.27. 
Finally the vehicle reaches the surface at point d. In Fig. 8.27 the path a–b–c–d 
is for a given ballistic coefficient. If m/(CDS) is made larger, the vehicle pen -
etrates more deeply into the atmosphere before slowing down, as illustrated by 
path a–b–e–f. Thus, as suspected from an examination of Eq. (8.108), the bal -
listic coefficient is an important design aspect of entry vehicles.
The ballistic coefficient of an entry vehicle of a certain mass is determined 
primarily by its shape and surface area. An object that is dense and presents a 
small frontal area like an asteroid would have a relatively high ballistic coef -
ficient, which is why such objects entering our atmosphere tend to maintain 
very high velocities, and often burn up before hitting the ground. A lighter 
weight vehicle with a large blunt frontal area, like the Apollo capsule, on the 
other hand, would have a lower ballistic coefficient designed in such a way 
that it decelerates more gradually and sustains a lower heat load during entry. 
The equations that allow one to calculate these parameters quantitatively are 
included on the web site, but qualitatively there are a few important concepts 
that are worth recognizing. The deceleration and the heat transfer rate of an 
entry vehicle are a function of both the atmospheric density, which is increas -
ing during descent, and the velocity of the vehicle, which is decreasing during

where the maximum heating occurs. Additionally, there are a few fundamentals 
that a mission designer should know:
∙ more than anything else, the entry velocity, V E, will determine how stress -
ful the entry trajectory is on the spacecraft and its occupants, in terms of 
both structural loading and heat transfer;
∙ the parameter that a pilot has the most control over during entry is the 
flight path angle, γ, which can also very strongly affect the deceleration 
and heat load;
∙ entry heating is inversely related to the radius of the leading edge of the entry 
capsule, so to minimize entry heating, the vehicle must have a blunt nose.
8.10 HISTORICAL NOTE: KEPLER
The 16th century was a period of quandary for astronomy. The conservative 
line of scientific thought held the earth as the center of the universe, with the 
sun, planets, and stars revolving about it on various celestial spheres. This 
geocentric system was popular among the Greeks. Put into a somewhat ratio -
nal form by Claudius Ptolemy in the second century ad, this earth-centered 
system was adopted as the truth by the Church in western Europe and was 
carried through to the 16th century. However, about the time that Columbus 
was discovering America, a Polish scientist by the name of Nicolaus Copernicus 
was beginning to develop different ideas. Copernicus reasoned that the earth 
as well as all the other planets revolved around the sun in a heliocentric system. 
He established his line of thought in a main work titled Six Books Concerning 
the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, published in the year of his death, 1543. 
Here Copernicus was diplomatic with regard to Church dogma. He stated that 
his heliocentric theory was not new, having been held by a few early Greek 
astronomers, and also that he was just “postulating and theorizing,” not neces -
sarily speaking the absolute truth. However, it was clear that Copernicus person-
ally believed in what he wrote. Another astronomer, Giordano Bruno, who 
evangelized Copernicus’s theory, was not so diplomatic and was burned at the 
stake in 1600. Galileo Galilei took up the heliocentric banner in 1632 and was 
 ultimately exiled under guard for his heresy. Finally the Danish astronomer 
Tycho Brahe, while shunning a direct association with the controversial 
 heliocentric theory, spent virtually his complete life from 1546 to 1602 making 
astronomical observations of planet and star movements, resulting in spectacular 
improvements in the precision of existing knowledge.
Into this tenuous time Johannes Kepler was born in Württemberg, Germany, 
on December 27, 1571. By winning scholarships, he was able to finish elementary 
school and go on to the University of T übingen. There he was converted to the 
heliocentric theory by Michael Mastlin, a professor of astronomy. Later Kepler 

===== PDF PAGE 746 =====
 8.11 Historical Note: Newton and the Law of Gravitation 727
became a teacher of mathematics and an ardent astronomer. Through his writings 
about celestial motion, Kepler came to the attention of Tycho Brahe, who was 
now living in Prague. In 1599 Kepler went to Prague to work under Brahe, who 
died just two years later. Kepler stayed in Prague, extending and improving the 
existing tables of celestial movement. In 1627 he published his Rudolphine Tables, 
which were much more accurate than any existing tables at that time.
However, Kepler was also thinking and theorizing about his observations, 
attempting to bring reason and order to the movement of the heavenly bodies. 
For example, the heliocentric system of Copernicus assumed circular orbits of 
the planets about the sun, but Kepler’s accurate observations did not precisely 
fit circular motion. In 1609 he found that elliptical orbits fit his measurements 
exactly, giving rise to Kepler’s first law  (see Sec. 8.6). In the same year he 
induced that a line drawn from the sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in 
equal times— Kepler’s second law. His first and second laws were published 
in his book New Astronomy  in 1609. Nine years later he discovered that the 
square of the period of planetary orbits was proportional to the cube of the 
semimajor axis of the elliptical orbit— Kepler’s third law. This was published 
in 1618 in his book Epitome of the Copernican Astronomy.
Kepler’s impact on astronomy was massive; in fact, his work was the 
founding of modern astronomy. His contributions are all the more stunning 
because his laws were induced from empirical observation. Kepler did not have 
the tools developed later by Newton. Therefore, he could not derive his laws 
with the same finesse as we did in Sec. 8.5.
It is interesting to note that Kepler also wrote science fiction. In his book 
Somnium (Dream), Kepler describes a trip from the earth to the moon. Recogniz-
ing that the void of space would not support flight by wings, he had to resort to 
demons as a supernatural mode of propulsion. These demons would carry along 
humans, suitably anesthetized to survive the rigors of space travel. He described 
the moon in as much astronomical detail as was possible in that age, but he 
imagined moon creatures that lived in caves. Modern historians of science fiction 
literature believe that Kepler’s Somnium was really a vehicle to present his serious 
scientific ideas about the moon while attempting to avoid religious persecution. 
Somnium was published in 1634, four years after Kepler’s death.
Kepler spent his later life as a professor of mathematics in Linz. He died 
in Regensburg on November 15, 1630, leaving a legacy that reaches across the 
centuries to the astronautics of the present day.
8.11  HISTORICAL NOTE: NEWTON AND THE LAW 
OF GRAVITATION
Newton’s law of universal gravitation, Eq. (8.19), appears in every modern 
high school and college physics textbook; its existence is virtually taken for 
granted. Moreover, this equation is the very foundation for all modern astro -
nautical calculations of motion through space, as discussed throughout this 
chapter. However, the disarming simplicity of Eq. (8.19) and its commonplace 

===== PDF PAGE 747 =====
728 CHAPTER 8 Space Flight (Astronautics)
acceptance in classical physics belie the turmoil that swarmed about the con -
cept of gravity before and during the 17th century, when Newton lived.
The earliest ideas about “gravity” were advanced by Aristotle during the 
period around 350 bc. Believing that the four fundamental elements of the 
universe were earth, water, air, and fire, the Aristotelian school held that every -
thing in the universe had its appointed station and tended to return to this station 
if originally displaced. Objects made from “earth” held the lowest station, and 
thus heavy material objects would fall to the ground, seeking their proper status. 
In contrast, fire and air held a high station and would seek this status by rising 
toward the heavens. These ideas persisted until the age of Copernicus, when 
people began to look for more substantial explanations of gravity.
In 1600 the English scientist William Gilbert suggested that magnetism was 
the source of gravity and that the earth was nothing more than a gigantic lode -
stone. Kepler adopted these views, stating that gravity was “a mutual affection 
between cognate bodies tending toward union or conjunction, similar in kind to 
magnetism.” Kepler used this idea in an attempt to prove his laws of planetary 
motion (see Sec. 8.10) but was not successful in obtaining a quantitative law for 
the force of gravity. About the same time, the French scientist and mathematician 
René Descartes (who introduced the Cartesian coordinate system to the world of 
mathematics) proposed that gravity was the result of an astronomical fluid that 
was swirling in a vortex motion, pushing heavy objects toward the core of the 
vortex. Christian Huygens, a Dutch gentleman and amateur scientist, seemed to 
confirm Descartes’s theory in the laboratory; he set up a whirlpool of water in 
a bowl and observed that pebbles “gravitated” to the center of the bowl.
Into this confused state of affairs was born Isaac Newton at Woolsthorpe 
near Grantham, Lincolnshire, England, on December 25, 1642. Newton’s father 
died a few months before he was born, and Newton was raised by his grand -
mother. His education ultimately led to studies at Trinity College, Cambridge 
University, in 1661, where he quickly showed his genius for mathematics. In 
1666 he left Cambridge for his home in Woolsthorpe Manor to avoid the Great 
Plague of 1665–1666. It was here, at the fresh age of 24, that Newton made 
some of his discoveries and conclusions that were to revolutionize science and 
mathematics, not the least of which was the development of differential calcu -
lus. Also, Newton later maintained that during this stay in the country he 
deduced the law of centripetal force: that a body in circular motion experiences 
a radial force that varies inversely with the distance from the center. (In today’s 
language, the centripetal acceleration due to circular motion is equal to V 2/r, 
as shown in all elementary physics books.) From this result applied to Kepler’s 
third law, Newton further deduced that the force of gravity between two objects 
varies inversely as the square of the distance separating them, which led to the 
universal law of gravitation, as given by Eq. (8.19). However, Newton did not 
bother to publish immediately or otherwise announce his findings. The public 
was kept in the dark for another 30 years!
Throughout the history of science and engineering, there are numerous 
examples of ideas whose “time had come” and that were conceived by several 

===== PDF PAGE 748 =====
 8.12 Historical Note: Lagrange 729
different people almost simultaneously. The same Christian Huygens made 
experiments with pendulums and circular moving bodies that led to his discov -
ery of the law of centripetal force in 1673. With this, Robert Hooke (of Hooke’s 
law fame), Christopher Wren (later to become an internationally famous archi -
tect), and Edmund Halley (of Halley’s comet fame) all deduced the inverse 
square law of gravity in 1679. Hooke wrote to Newton in the same year, telling 
him of the inverse square discovery and asking Newton to use it to prove that 
a planet revolves in an elliptical orbit. Newton did not reply. In 1685 the prob -
lem was again posed to Newton, this time by Halley. Newton sent back such a 
proof. Halley was much impressed and strongly encouraged Newton to publish 
all his discoveries and thinking as soon as possible. This lead to Newton’s 
Philosophiae Naturales Principia Mathematica—the famous Principia—which 
has become the foundation of classical physics. It is interesting to note that the 
Principia was originally to be published by the Royal Society. But Hooke, who 
laid claim to the prior discovery of the inverse square law and who was the 
curator of the Royal Society, apparently discouraged such publication. Instead 
the Principia, the most important scientific document of that time in history, 
was published at the personal expense of Halley.
8.12 HISTORICAL NOTE: LAGRANGE
In Sec. 8.3, a corollary to Newton’s second law was introduced: Lagrange’s 
equation. Lagrange came after Newton. He was one of the small group of 
European scientists and mathematicians who worked to develop and augment 
Newtonian (classical) physics during the 18th century; he was a contemporary 
of Laplace and a friend of Leonhard Euler.
Joseph L. Lagrange was born of French parents at Turin, Italy, on January 
25, 1736. His father was an officer in the French army; hence it is no surprise 
that at the age of 19 Lagrange was appointed as professor of mathematics at 
the Turin Artillery School. Active in scientific thought, he helped to found the 
Turin Academy of Sciences. In 1756 he wrote to Euler (see Sec. 4.22) with 
some original contributions to the calculus of variations. This helped to estab -
lish Lagrange’s reputation. In fact, in 1766 he replaced Euler as director of the 
Berlin Academy at the invitation of Frederick II (Frederick the Great) of Prus -
sia. For the next 20 years, Lagrange was extremely productive in the field of 
mechanics. His work was analytical, and he endeavored to reduce the many 
aspects of mechanics to a few general formulas. This is clearly reflected in the 
formalism discussed in Sec. 8.3. Lagrange’s equations used in Sec. 8.3 were 
published in an important book by Lagrange titled Mécanique Analytique  in 
1787. For these contributions, he is considered by some historians to be the 
greatest mathematician of the 18th century.
Lagrange moved to Paris in 1786. During the French Revolution, he was 
president of the committee for reforming weights and measures standards. At 
the time of his death in Paris on April 10, 1813, he was working on a revised 
version of his Mécanique Analytique.

===== PDF PAGE 749 =====
730 CHAPTER 8 Space Flight (Astronautics)
8.13  HISTORICAL NOTE: UNMANNED  
SPACE FLIGHT
On the evening of October 4, 1957, the present author (Dr. Anderson) was a 
student of aeronautical engineering. The radio was on. Concentration on studies 
was suddenly interrupted by a news bulletin: The Soviet Union had just suc -
cessfully launched the first artificial earth satellite in history. Labeled Sputnik I 
and shown in Fig. 8.28, this 184-lb sphere circled the earth in an elliptical orbit, 
with an apogee and perigee of 560 and 140 mi, respectively, and with a period 
of 1.5 h. The personal feeling of exhilaration that humanity had finally made 
the first great step toward space exploration was tempered by questions about 
the technical position of the United States in space flight  relative to that of the 
Soviet Union. These feelings were to be reflected and amplified throughout the 
United States for weeks, months, and years to come. Sputnik I started a tech -
nological revolution that has influenced virtually all aspects of society, from 
education to business, from biology to philosophy. October 4, 1957, is a red-
letter date in the history of humanity—the beginning of the space age.
Although the launching of Sputnik I came as a surprise to most of the general 
public, the technical community of the Western world had been given some clear 
hints by Russian scientists. For example, on November 27, 1953, at the World 
Peace Council in Vienna, the Soviet academician A. N. Nesmeyanov stated that 
“science had reached such a stage that  .  .  .  the creation of an artificial satellite 
Figure 8.28 The first artificial earth satellite— Sputnik I—
launched on October 4, 1957.
(Source: Courtesy of John Anderson .)


===== PDF PAGE 750 =====
 8.13 Historical Note: Unmanned Space Flight 731
of the earth is a real possibility.” Then, in April 1955, the U.S.S.R. Academy of 
Sciences announced the creation of the Permanent Interdepartmental Commis -
sion for Interplanetary Communications, with responsibility for developing 
artificial earth satellites for meteorological applications. In August of that year, 
the highly respected Russian scientist Leonid I. Sedov, at the Sixth International 
Astronautical Congress in Copenhagen, said, “In my opinion, it will be possible 
to launch an artificial satellite of the Earth within the next two years, and there 
is the technological possibility of creating artificial satellites of various sizes and 
weights.” Obviously the Russian program kept to its schedule. Indeed, in June 
1957, just four months before Sputnik I, the same A. N. Nesmeyanov blatantly 
stated that both the rocket launch vehicle and the satellite were ready and would 
be launched in a few months. Clear signs and clear words—yet the launching of 
Sputnik I still fell like a ton of bricks on the Western world.
In 1957 the United States was not new to the idea of artificial satellites. 
Indeed, some farsighted thinking and technical analyses of the prospects for 
launching such satellites were performed by the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Army 
Air Force beginning in 1945. Then, in May 1946 (just one year after Germany 
had been defeated in World War II), a Project RAND report titled “Preliminary 
Design of an Experimental World-Circling Spaceship” was submitted to Wright 
Field, Dayton, Ohio. This report showed the feasibility of putting a 500-lb 
satellite in orbit at around 300 mi high. Moreover, it outlined how this could 
be accomplished in a five-year time scale! The authors of this report made 
some prophetic statements:
Although the crystal ball is cloudy, two things seem clear—1. A satellite vehicle 
with appropriate instrumentation can be expected to be one of the most potent 
scientific tools of the Twentieth Century.
2. The achievement of a satellite craft by the United States would inflame the 
imagination of mankind, and would probably produce repercussions in the world 
comparable to the explosion of the atomic bomb. . . .
Then the authors went on to state,
Since mastery of the elements is a reliable index of material progress, the nation 
which first makes significant achievements in space travel will be acknowledged 
as the world leader in both military and scientific techniques. To visualize the 
impact on the world, one can imagine the consternation and admiration that would 
be felt here if the United States were to discover suddenly that some other nation 
had already put up a successful satellite.
These were indeed prophetic words, written fully 11 years before Sputnik I.
The 1946 RAND report, along with several contemporary technical reports 
from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology, 
established some fundamental engineering principles and designs for rocket 
launch vehicles and satellites. However, these ideas were not seized upon by the 
U.S. government. The period after World War II was one of shrinking defense 
budgets, and money was simply not available for such a space venture. Of prob-
ably greater importance was the lack of a mission. What if a satellite were 

===== PDF PAGE 751 =====
732 CHAPTER 8 Space Flight (Astronautics)
launched? What benefits would it bring, especially military benefits? Keep in 
mind that this was in a period before miniaturized electronics and sophisticated 
sensing and telemetering equipment. Therefore, the first serious U.S. effort to 
establish a satellite program withered on the vine, and the idea lay essentially 
dormant for the next nine years.
Although upstaged by Sputnik I, the United States in 1957 finally did have 
an ongoing project to orbit an artificial satellite. On July 29, 1955, President 
Dwight D. Eisenhower announced that the United States would orbit a small 
earth satellite in conjunction with the International Geophysical Year. Making 
use of 10 years of high-altitude sounding rocket technology, which started with 
a number of captured German V-2 rockets, the United States established the 
Vangard program, managed by the Office of Naval Research, to accomplish this 
goal. Martin Company in Baltimore, Maryland, was chosen as the prime con -
tractor. During the next two years, a rocket booster was designed and built to 
launch a small, 3-lb experimental satellite. By government edict, the Vangard 
project was required not to draw upon or interface with the rapidly growing and 
high-priority ICBM program, which was developing large rocket engines for 
the military. Therefore, Dr. John P. Hagen, director of Project Vangard, and his 
small team of scientists and engineers had to struggle almost as second-class 
citizens to design the Vangard rocket in an atmosphere of relatively low priority. 
(This is in sharp contrast to the Russian space program, which from the very 
beginning utilized and benefited from the Soviet military ICBM developments. 
Because Russian atomic warheads of that day were heavier than comparable 
U.S. devices, the Soviet Union had to develop more powerful rocket boosters. 
Their space program correspondingly benefited, allowing Sputnik I and II to be 
the surprisingly large weights of 184 and 1120 lb, respectively.)
By October 1957 two Vangard rockets had been successfully tested at 
Cape Canaveral, and the test program, which was aimed at putting a satellite 
into orbit before the end of 1958, was reasonably close to schedule. Then 
came Sputnik I on October 4. Not to be completely upstaged, the White House 
announced on October 11 that Project Vangard would launch a U.S. satellite 
“in the near future.” Suddenly in the limelight of public attention, and now 
under intense political pressure, a third test rocket was successfully tested  
on October 23, carrying a 4000-lb dummy payload to an altitude of 109 and 
335 mi downrange. Then, on December 6, 1957, in full view of the world’s 
press, the first Vangard was prepared to put a small satellite into orbit. Unfor -
tunately, the Vangard first-stage engine had its first (and last) failure of the 
program. With failing thrust, the rocket lifted a few feet off the launch pad 
and then fell back in a spectacular explosion. In Dr. Hagen’s words, “Although 
we had three successful test launches in a row, the failure of TV-3 [the des -
ignation of that particular vehicle] was heard around the world.”
Despite the original disadvantages of low priority, the emotional pressure 
after Sputnik I, and the inglorious failure of December 6, the Vangard project 
went on to be very successful. Vangards I, II,  and III were put into orbit on 
March 17, 1958, February 17, 1959, and September 18, 1959, respectively, 
attributing to the fine efforts of Dr. Hagen and his group.

===== PDF PAGE 752 =====
But Vangard I was not the first U.S. satellite. President Eisenhower’s July 
1955 announcement about U.S. plans to orbit a satellite was followed by much 
debate about whether military rocketry should be used. One proposal at the 
time was to use the rocket vehicles being developed at the Army’s Redstone 
Arsenal at Huntsville, Alabama, under the technical direction of Dr. Wernher 
Von Braun. After the decision was made to go with the Vangard, the engineers 
at the Army Ballistic Missile Agency at Huntsville continued to propose a 
satellite program using the proven intermediate-range Jupiter C rocket. All 
such proposals were turned down. However, the picture changed after Sputnik. 
In later October 1957, Von Braun’s group was given the green light to orbit 
a satellite: the target date was January 30, 1958. A fourth stage was added to 
the Jupiter C rocket; this new configuration was labeled the Juno I. The target 
date was missed by only one day. On January 31, 1958, Explorer I , the first 
U.S. artificial satellite, was placed into orbit by Von Braun’s team of scientists 
and engineers from Huntsville. Explorer I, shown in Fig. 8.29, weighed 18 lb, 
and its orbit had apogee and perigee of 957 and 212 mi, respectively; its period 
was 115 min. With the launchings of both Sputnik I  and Explorer I,  the two 
technological giants in the world—the United States and the Soviet Union—
were now competing in the space arena .
Figure 8.29 Explorer I, the first U.S. artificial earth 
satellite, launched on January 31, 1958.
(Source: NASA.)
